title: Lagaan Turns 25 and Returns to Theaters This Week. The Stories Behind Its Soundtrack Are Even Better Than You Remember.
excerpt: At Spotify's first-ever live 'Behind the Beats' recording, Aamir Khan, A.R. Rahman, Javed Akhtar, and Ashutosh Gowariker spilled secrets about the album that defined a generation — and announced a three-day theatrical re-release starting June 12.
body:
There are songs that belong to certain seasons and certain cities. And then there are songs that belong to everyone, everywhere, all at once. The opening bars of 'Chale Chalo' fall into that second category. So does every other track on the Lagaan soundtrack.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=hTt5FbgziPw

Twenty-five years after Aamir Khan and Ashutosh Gowariker convinced an entire country to care about a cricket match they already knew the ending of, Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India is returning to theaters — a limited three-day run from June 12 to 14 across India, announced by Aamir Khan Productions on Instagram. And if you're in London this summer, clear your calendar: the film screens at BFI IMAX on July 12, followed by a rare Aamir Khan in-conversation session at BFI Southbank on July 16 as part of the London Indian Film Festival's 17th edition.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZHaOT0gGnv/

But before the projectors fire up again, the people who made the magic sat together for one of the most revealing conversations about Indian film music in recent memory.

Behind the Beats — and the Arguments

At Spotify's first-ever live recording of 'Behind the Beats', Aamir Khan, composer A.R. Rahman, lyricist Javed Akhtar, and Gowariker gathered to pull apart the album song by song — and what emerged was a portrait of creative tension, ego, and genius colliding in the best possible way.

Take 'Ghanan Ghanan,' the first song Aamir ever heard from the film.

"It blew me away. There's an excitement in the movement and tempo of the song. It has the joy of the rain finally coming; it takes you on a ride, and once it's over, you realise that the clouds have gone away and there's no rain. I can't think of any other song that takes you on a journey like this one." — Aamir Khan

Gowariker revealed that Rahman's process was unlike anything he'd encountered: instead of presenting a tune or melody, Rahman handed over three hours' worth of music and asked them to choose the parts they liked. Three hours. For one film.

Then there's 'O Rey Chhori,' the playful romantic track that almost didn't exist as we know it. Rahman admitted the tune was originally composed for his patriotic album Maa Tujhe Salaam, not for Lagaan at all — and it was slower. Too slow for Aamir's taste.

"He told me Karan Johar's film is releasing around the same time and that he has amazing romantic songs. He asked me, 'What have you done?'" — A.R. Rahman

The song was sped up. Crisis averted. And here's a detail that might rattle your inner film nerd: the English lyrics in that track were written by Farhan and Zoya Akhtar, back when they were still benefiting from, as their father Javed put it, being "educated and sent to college."

The most legendary near-miss belongs to 'Chale Chalo.' Before Javed Akhtar wrote the lyrics that would eventually name the making-of documentary, Rahman had been humming a placeholder: Nasha Nasha. Aamir and Gowariker got addicted to it. They went to Akhtar and told him to write whatever he wanted — just don't change those two words.

Akhtar refused.

"There is no rain, the farmers are starving to death, they must pay three times the lagaan — and the producer and director are asking me to use the words 'Nasha Nasha.' If it weren't for me, that documentary would have been called 'Nasha Nasha.'" — Javed Akhtar

And then there's the one that humbled even an atheist. Akhtar called 'O Paalanhaare' the most challenging song he ever wrote — precisely because Rahman's composition was so pure it didn't sound man-made.

"You can play it to an Eskimo, or someone from Manhattan or Moscow — everyone can tell you it's a tune of devotion. Even as an atheist, I had to find innocence and surrender in my heart. You can't write such songs with tact and craft; it can only be done with purity and simplicity." — Javed Akhtar

Rahman, for his part, was thinking about permanence. "I wanted to make the music timeless, and luckily it has become that. But timeless music needs timeless singers, and that's how we approached Lata ji and Asha ji."

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For millions of NRIs, Lagaan wasn't just a film — it was the one movie your parents, your aunties, and eventually your non-Indian friends all agreed was incredible. It was India's answer at the Oscars, one of only a handful of Indian films ever nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. It remains the moment many in the West first took Indian cinema seriously outside of arthouse.

The BFI IMAX screening in London gives the UK diaspora something the original release couldn't: a 2026-grade projection of a film designed for the big screen, where the cricket sequences and Rahman's score can do what they were always meant to do.

As Aamir Khan put it: "To see Lagaan still connect with audiences across generations and across geographies is very special."

Twenty-five years. The songs haven't aged a day.
